The passage reports medical problems in study participants. In Phase 1, a few participants had temporary lymphocyte drops 1 to 3 days after Dose 1 of BNT162b1 or BNT162b2; counts returned to normal by 6 to 8 days, and none had low lymphocytes 6 to 8 days after Dose 2. Injection site reactions within 7 days were well tolerated, mostly mild or moderate, and pain was most common. Systemic events within 7 days were also well tolerated, mostly mild or moderate, with tiredness and headache most common. Within 1 month after Dose 2 or boosters, Phase 1 doses of BNT162b1 and BNT162b2 at 10, 20, and 30 µg were well tolerated except BNT162b1 at 100 µg, which was stopped after Dose 1 because of injection site reactions or systemic events. No Phase 1 participants left because of medical problems, most problems were mild or moderate, and no single problem occurred in more than 2 participants in any dose group. In Phase 2/3, 30 µg BNT162b2 was well tolerated; less than 1% of BNT162b2 and placebo groups left the blinded phase because of medical problems; most problems were mild or moderate and mostly involved injection site reactions or systemic events. No single medical problem occurred in more than 1% of participants aged 12 to 15. Serious medical problems in Phase 1 included inflamed appendix in the BNT162b2 20-µg group and inflamed nerves in the 30-µg group, which researchers did not believe were related to the vaccine; no BNT162b1 or placebo recipients had serious problems. Phase 2/3 had few serious problems, with no single problem in at least 1% of participants; some in those aged 16 and older may be related to the study vaccine. Booster serious problems were few and not believed related. No participant died in Phase 1. In Phase 2/3, deaths occurred among BNT162b2 recipients, placebo-then-BNT162b2 recipients, and placebo recipients; causes varied and researchers do not believe BNT162b2 caused them. No Phase 3 participant died among those who received BNT162b2SA without prior BNT162b2. More information is available from the study site, protocol, and full scientific report.

Neutral particle diagnostics are discussed for measuring the ion distribution function in the core of a tokamak, where fusion occurs. Electron cyclotron emission gives Te rather than Ti; laser-induced fluorescence cannot be used because core particles are fully ionized; and Thomson scattering gives the electron distribution. The method considered uses core ions that become neutrals, escape confinement, and are detected outside, carrying information about the ion distribution. Two issues are neutral production and neutral transport.

Neutral production can occur by charge exchange with edge neutrals or with an injected neutral beam. Neutral transport is limited by re-ionization through electron impact ionization, ion impact ionization, and charge exchange with ions. Charge exchange is resonant and likely. The escape probability is an exponential of a line integral of an attenuation coefficient. With Vi << VA << Ve, the attenuation simplifies; for energetic neutrals, the electron term can be neglected, leaving approximately (sigma_p + sigma_C)ni. For 10 keV neutrals and density around 10^20 m^-3, the mean free path is about 10 cm, so in a roughly 100 cm reactor few neutrals escape. Diagnostics require line-integrated density below about 10^19 m^-2, giving a mean free path near a meter and requiring relatively low-density devices.

Edge fueling can produce detectable core neutrals; radiative recombination is negligible. Passive charge exchange with edge neutrals uses a stripping cell, magnetic bending, and detector bins to measure the distribution, yielding core ion temperature and fast-ion tails, but it is line-integrated. A neutral beam provides active, localized measurement through charge exchange in the overlap of the beam and detector view. Charge exchange recombination spectroscopy uses the beam to charge-exchange with fully stripped impurities, producing excited impurity photons; it measures impurity density from intensity and ion temperature and flow from Doppler broadening and shift, with issues from edge impurities, Bremsstrahlung background, and weak signal, mitigated by beam modulation.

Beam emission spectroscopy observes excitation of beam neutrals; line intensity is proportional to electron density, so it measures density fluctuations and turbulent transport, but requires accounting for relevant processes and beam attenuation. Motional Stark effect uses the electric field −V×B seen by beam particles, causing linear Stark splitting of energy levels. Transitions such as H-alpha produce multiple polarization-dependent lines; the splitting is larger than Zeeman splitting and can be used to determine magnetic field angle and the poloidal field or current profile.

Toyota’s Walt Bernstein was frustrated in late 2004 with ChassisCo’s Athens, Georgia plant, which supplied rear suspension cradles for the new Suprima crossover. After 14 months of production, output was about 60% of target, sourced parts were frequently nonconforming, and problem tracking was weak. Toyota had sent engineering, project management, stamping, welding, and automation experts, but improvement was insufficient and the vehicle program was at risk.

The passage describes Toyota Production System and Just-in-Time as integrated systems based on jidoka, just-in-time, continuous improvement, and respect for people. Toyota chose ChassisCo for the 1997 Suprima, later the 1999 Responsa, and gave it more responsibility for the 2003 Suprima, including sourcing 85 parts and project management. The Athens plant increased automation from 13 to 102 robots and doubled welding, but ChassisCo lacked project management, parts tracking, supplier management, tuning capability, and resources. Its decentralization, numerous global launches, aggressive target pricing, low supplier bids, and logistics errors contributed to problems. Toyota did not recognize the capability gaps or second-tier problems in time.

The 2003 Suprima launched on time in September 2003 but at low volume and with high defects, downtime, scrap, and inventories. A March 2004 Toyota audit found out-of-conformance assembly-critical welds; a November arc welding audit scored 13%; external defects rose. Bernstein visited Athens frequently and Toyota provided support, but weak quality information, no defect flowout control, overtime, and possible burnout threatened a downward spiral. ChassisCo’s McDonald asked for a significant price increase; Bernstein said the issue was more a quality concern and that Toyota needed a breakthrough.

The passage discusses PBPK modeling for radiopharmaceutical therapies within computational nuclear oncology and theranostic digital twins. PBPK models describe radiotheranostic agent activity over time, use patient-specific inputs, support dosimetry and dosing optimization, and can link pharmacokinetics with radiobiology to predict exposure-response. Models can be built using bottom-up, top-down, or middle-out approaches. The passage outlines VVUQ: verification confirms correct implementation; validation assesses internal and external predictive performance using goodness-of-fit, model selection, sensitivity analysis, and prediction evaluation; uncertainty quantification characterizes parameter and output precision and accuracy. Extending PBPK to dynamic TDTs raises challenges from continuous imaging and clinical data integration, temporal variability, and sparse or noisy inputs. PBPK models in RPTs remain underdeveloped from a regulatory perspective, and fit-for-purpose VVUQ frameworks are needed for clinical translation and integration.

McGill University researchers developed an AI tool called DOLPHIN that detects previously invisible disease markers inside single cells by analyzing exons and junction reads beyond gene-level methods. The tool may help doctors detect diseases earlier, match patients to therapies, and build virtual cell models to simulate disease and drug responses, with next steps expanding it to millions of cells.

The passage addresses persuasion’s role in economic and political systems and concerns about large language models’ persuasive capabilities. It notes challenges in measuring LLM persuasiveness due to inconsistent evaluations and heterogeneous effects. To address this, it proposes a theory-driven framework based on Bayesian persuasion, viewing LLM persuasiveness as a Sender’s strategic information revelation to shift a Receiver’s beliefs. It repurposes human-human persuasion datasets to create evaluation and training environments, conducts a 45-participant human study, and tests frontier models, finding stronger models achieve higher persuasion gains and more adaptive information revelation. It also uses reinforcement learning to train Sender LLMs against Receiver LLMs, showing that small Llama3.2-3B-Instruct models can improve strategic persuasion comparably to large LLMs, with transfer to different Receiver architectures. Key contributions include the framework, concrete environments, and empirical evidence that frontier models can exhibit strong persuasive capabilities improvable via reinforcement learning.

The passage describes NVIDIA’s Turing GPU architecture, focusing on TU102, with TU104 and TU106 as scaled variants. TU102 includes six GPCs, 36 TPCs, and 72 SMs; each SM has 64 CUDA Cores, eight Tensor Cores, one RT Core, a 256 KB register file, four texture units, and 96 KB L1/shared memory. The full TU102 has 12 32-bit GDDR6 memory controllers, 96 ROPs, 6144 KB L2 cache, and 144 FP64 units. Turing’s SM supports concurrent FP32 and INT32 execution, independent thread scheduling, and unified shared memory/L1/texture caching. Tensor Cores add FP16, INT8, and INT4 modes. Turing supports GDDR6, memory compression, new display/video engines, USB-C/VirtualLink, and second-generation NVLink on TU102/TU104. RT Cores accelerate BVH traversal and ray/triangle intersection for real-time ray tracing, using hybrid rendering, denoising, and BVH acceleration. NGX enables DLSS, InPainting, AI Slow-Mo, and AI Super Rez. Other features include mesh shading, variable rate shading, texture space shading, multi-view rendering, and resource management. TU104 has six GPCs, 48 SMs, 3072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, 48 RT Cores, and one NVLink link. TU106 has three GPCs, 36 SMs, 2304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, 36 RT Cores, and no NVLink or SLI. RTX-OPS is described as a workload-based metric. Appendix material covers ray tracing basics.

The passage covers DLSS 4, Blackwell architecture, neural shaders, RTX neural rendering features, and Blackwell GPUs. DLSS 4 Multi Frame Generation builds on Ada frame generation, using Blackwell hardware and DLSS software innovations to generate up to three additional frames per traditionally rendered frame. Its new frame-generation AI model is 40% faster and uses 30% less VRAM than the prior method, runs once per rendered frame, replaces hardware optical flow with an AI model, and uses enhanced Flip Metering with the Blackwell display engine for pacing. Blackwell-only features include 5th Gen Tensor Cores and the AI Management Processor.

DLSS 4 introduces transformer-based models for Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and DLAA, trained by NVIDIA supercomputers. Compared with CNN models, transformers use self-attention, identify longer-range patterns, scale to 2x more parameters, and improve stability, lighting detail, motion, ghosting, anti-aliasing, and challenging lighting.

The passage also describes neural shaders as an evolution of shader technology, with Blackwell introducing developer-created neural shaders. The Cooperative Vectors API for DX12 and Vulkan lets Tensor Cores be accessed through shaders, enabling neural texture compression, RTX Neural Materials, Neural Radiance Cache, RTX Skin, and RTX Neural Faces. Neural Texture Compression is described as saving over 3x memory in a demo; NRC caches and approximates radiance and trains on live game data; RTX Skin is the first ray-traced example of subsurface scattering in games; RTX Neural Faces uses a real-time generative AI model from rasterized face and 3D pose data.

Finally, the passage lists Blackwell GPUs: GB202 flagship with 92.2 billion transistors, 12 GPCs, 96 TPCs, 192 SMs, 512-bit memory controllers, 24,576 CUDA Cores, and RTX 5090; GB203 high-end with 45.6 billion transistors, 7 GPCs, 42 TPCs, 84 SMs, 256-bit memory, and RTX 5080/5070 Ti; GB205 performance segment with 31 billion transistors, 5 GPCs, 50 SMs, 192-bit memory, and RTX 5070.

This application claims priority to U.S. patent application Ser. No. 16/985,649, filed Aug. 5, 2020. Embodiments relate generally to vehicles and to a variable multiplexer for vehicle communication bus compatibility. Vehicles may use a communication bus, such as CAN bus, and a data link connector, such as an OBD port, to connect external devices. Although many manufacturers use a standardized data link connector, pinout configurations may vary, so different cables are used for compatibility. Disclosed are systems, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media for a variable multiplexer that can be electronically configured to a desired pinout configuration to provide compatibility with a given vehicle using a single standardized cable. The device may determine the pinout configuration by providing a vehicle identifier, such as a VIN, to a remote computing system that maintains a vehicle data index and returns pinout data. It may also use a listening mode to gather data transmitted across the communication bus and compare data received at pins to known pinout configurations. In some embodiments, a checksum value is used to verify data against known pinout configurations. The external device may include a variable multiplexer, network gateway device, connection detection component, pinout configuration determination component, pinout configuration modification component, and data storage. Methods include detecting connection to a communication bus, determining a pinout configuration, and configuring the variable multiplexer. Additional passages describe software architecture and machine components.

The passage states that equality is a historically shaped concept enriched by opportunity, political, racial, social, economic, and gender equality, and defined as a moral and social ideal and a principle of non-discrimination. Education is defined as a process that shapes and changes individuals, exists at every level of life, and is important for human development and social order. Equality of opportunity in education is defined as non-discriminatory access to educational services and conditions, regardless of family or economic origin, and consideration of individual needs. It is affected by economic, geographical, political, individual, and social factors. In Turkey, the Ministry of National Education and National Education Councils shape education, and reasons equality came to the fore include inadequate schools, economic difficulties, lack of equipment, and lack of motivation from cultural and social factors. The conclusion notes disagreement about what equal opportunity requires but accepts that educational opportunities should be equal, based on individual abilities and needs, with early measurement, improved access and quality, teacher quality, and preschool expansion.

The passage discusses reusable shared components and patterns for computer programming and distributed systems. It explains that patterns enable reusable components and focuses on container-based patterns. Single-node patterns include sidecar, where a sidecar container augments an application container; ambassador, where an ambassador brokers interactions such as sharded services, service brokering, and request splitting; and adapter, which modifies an application container’s interface for monitoring, logging, or health checks. It also covers multi-node patterns: microservices, replicated stateless load-balanced services, readiness probes, session-tracked services, application-layer replicated services, caching layers, rate limiting, SSL termination, and sharded services. It describes sharded caches, replicated sharded caches, sharding functions, hashing, determinism, uniformity, and selection of shard keys. Deployment examples use Kubernetes, Docker, Redis, memcache, nginx, twemproxy, Prometheus, and fluentd.

The passage describes NVIDIA’s RTX Blackwell architecture and features. Blackwell GB20x GPUs double many integer operations by unifying INT32 and FP32 cores, though unified cores operate as either FP32 or INT32 per clock cycle, and not all INT operations achieve 2x speedups. Ada SM was optimized for standard shaders; Blackwell SM for neural shaders. Texture units increase from 512 in RTX 4090 to 680 in RTX 5090, with RTX 5090 delivering 1636.76 Gigatexels/sec versus 1290.2 on RTX 4090; Blackwell SM also doubles point-sampling texture performance per cycle.

Blackwell introduces GDDR7 with PAM3 signaling, including 28 Gbps GDDR7 on RTX 5090 with 1.792 TB/sec peak bandwidth and 30 Gbps on RTX 5080 with 960 GB/sec. GDDR7 includes built-in ECC and EDR support. Tensor Cores support FP16, BF16, TF32, INT8, Hopper’s FP8 Transformer Engine, plus new FP4, FP6, and Second-Generation FP8 Transformer Engine. Fourth-generation RT Cores double ray-triangle throughput and add Mega Geometry, Triangle Cluster Intersection Engine, and Linear Swept Spheres. Mega Geometry includes CLAS, PTLAS, and subdivision surfaces; LSS accelerates hair rendering. SER 2.0 improves reordering, and AMP is a RISC-V context scheduler. Video features include 4:2:2 H.264/HEVC encode/decode, ninth-generation NVENC, sixth-generation NVDEC, and DisplayPort 2.1b. Power efficiency includes advanced power gating, accelerated frequency switching, and low latency sleep. DLSS 4 adds Multi Frame Generation and transformer models for Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and DLAA. Neural shaders include RTX Neural Materials, Neural Texture Compression, Neural Radiance Cache, RTX Skin, and RTX Neural Faces. The passage also lists GB202, GB203, and GB205 GPUs and RTX 50-series specifications.

Building a defensive wall in soccer means placing defenders shoulder-to-shoulder to block the goal from a nearby free kick, usually about 10 yards from the ball and often just outside the Penalty Area. It becomes important when players can shoot accurately and strongly from close range, usually around age 12 on a full-sized field. The wall blocks roughly half the goal, giving the goalkeeper more reaction time; defenders cut the near-side angle while the goalkeeper covers the far side. The goalkeeper decides whether to build a wall based on ball location and experience, and the number of wall players depends on distance and angle, from as few as two to as many as five, up to eight. Under Law 13, the ball is stationary, defenders must be at least 10 yards away unless on their own goal line, quick free kicks may be taken, and for walls of three or more attackers must remain at least 1 m away. Referees need not allow time to build a wall, and delaying restarts or blocking the ball can result in yellow cards. A traditional wall uses an Anchor/Post-man positioned on the line from the near post to the ball, 10 yards away, directed by the goalkeeper or a wall setter with left/right step calls and a “Hold” signal; other players fill in shoulder-to-shoulder. Players face the ball, avoid gaps, may protect certain body parts, may jump, and must react after the kick. Rare indirect free kicks less than 10 yards from goal require players to stand on the goal line between the posts. The passage also gives coaching tips and an alternative of not using a wall.

The reverse play is a high-risk, high-reward football play designed to deceive the defense by running in one direction before giving the ball to another player running opposite. In a traditional reverse, the quarterback hands or tosses to a running back or wide receiver, who then tosses to a crossing wide receiver; blockers form a seal. An example is the 2018 Carolina Panthers against Tampa Bay, with Cam Newton to DJ Moore, then Curtis Samuel for a big gain and eventual touchdown. Variations include the fake reverse, shown by the 2020 Arizona Cardinals with Kyler Murray faking to his running back and Andy Isabella before running himself; the reverse screen, shown by 2021 Purdue against Michigan State, ending in a screen and touchdown; and the reverse pass, where the quarterback becomes a passing option and catches the ball for a touchdown.

The passage presents IDC findings on technology trends in industrial development and manufacturing. It describes data visualization and engineering workstations “as a Service” from datacenters using a common data pool, visualization, and cloud technologies, combined with AR/VR, to improve team access and collaborative design. The administrator of Melvin Douglas’s estate appealed a district court ruling that Farmway Credit Union could exhaust its security interest in the decedent’s personal property without filing a claim in the estate or foreclosing in district court. Douglas had defaulted on debts secured by farm machinery, equipment, crops, livestock, and real estate. Before his death, Douglas and his wife orally agreed that Farmway could sell the personal property collateral at public sale; after his death, his heirs followed through. Farmway held the sale, gave notice, applied proceeds to the debt, harvested wheat, and sold cattle after notice. The administrator sought declaratory judgment and possession. The district court granted summary judgment for Farmway, finding no conflict between the administrator’s statutory right to possession and Farmway’s self-help repossession. On appeal, the court held the administrator’s right was not absolute and was affected by the decedent’s lifetime contracts. Because Farmway had a security agreement and a pre-death agreement allowing disposition of collateral, with heirs cooperating, the court affirmed. It did not decide broader self-help issues absent such agreement. The court also found summary judgment was proper because the pertinent facts were uncontroverted and no discovery remained relevant.

Its strengths include exploiting an aggressive, overpursuing defense, creating bad angles, and getting more bodies to the point of attack. Its weaknesses include longer development, vulnerability to defensive penetration, and being spilled laterally. The passage details Counter Trey assignments against 3-4 Odd and 4-3 Even fronts, plus variations: Singleback GT Counter and Gun Split GT Counter Triple Option.

The paper introduces a mathematical framework for investigating cubic-to-tetragonal (CT) phase coexistence in ferroelectrics using high-resolution X-ray diffraction 3D reciprocal space mapping. It extends adaptive state (AS) and Weschler–Lieberman–Read (WLR) crystallographic concepts, modeling CT coexistence through periodic assemblages of tetragonal domains connected by permissible domain walls and mismatch-free habit planes to the cubic phase. The model uses a domain volume ratio ω, catalogs 24 ASC variants, and predicts Bragg peak splitting. Unlike conventional AS assumptions, it does not necessarily require domain miniaturization and assumes T-domains can diffract independently while preserving ASC orientation relationships. Predictions are compared with experimental reciprocal space maps of PMN-35PT at the CT transition, showing agreement with modeled ASC variants. Domain sizes are estimated as several hundred nanometers, without excluding possible miniaturization near the transition. The formalism is proposed for diffraction analysis and other coexisting ferroelectric phases.

BA.2.86 (Pirola) was first detected in late July 2023 in Denmark and was classified by WHO as a variant of interest; an outbreak in a UK elderly care home had an 86.6% attack rate. The study used pseudo-virus neutralization assays with sera from 30 healthcare workers before and after BNT162b2 XBB.1.5 vaccination. BA.2.86 and its derivative JN.1 escaped neutralization in double-boostered individuals, with JN.1 escape more pronounced before booster vaccination. The XBB.1.5 booster increased neutralizing titers against both to comparable levels, reduced the gap to BA.2, and eliminated it between JN.1 and BA.2.86, though titers remained lower than BA.2. A reverse mutational scanning library of 33 single BA.2.86 reversion mutants identified ins16MPLF, K356T, N460K, V483Δ, A484K, F486P, and P621S as contributing to neutralizing antibody escape. After the XBB.1.5 booster, deletion of the MPLF insertion at position 16, reinsertion of Y144, and reversions K544E, S621P, and K484A improved neutralization. Limitations include use of pseudo-viruses, lack of hybrid immunity information, and analysis of only single mutants.

This study investigated elementary school mathematics teachers’ views in the UAE on using distance education (DE) to teach mathematics to grades 1–5. A quantitative online questionnaire was distributed in spring 2020–2021 to 90 private and governmental school teachers in Al Ain. It measured perceptions, obstacles, and future preferences. Results showed generally positive perceptions: teachers felt able to use digital technologies, adapt lessons, and represent mathematical ideas. They were skeptical that online teaching is more suitable than face-to-face for elementary mathematics. Obstacles included increased instructional preparation time, stress, the need for new teaching methods, and concerns about student communication, motivation, learning, and participation; school resources and training were generally reported as available. Most teachers preferred face-to-face teaching in the future, though a significant percentage enjoyed teaching mathematics online. Obstacles differed significantly by educational level, favoring graduates; no significant differences in perceptions were found by gender or years of experience. The study concluded that tailored support and training are needed for DE.

MITOCW lecture covers Langmuir probes. A Langmuir probe is a metal conductor inserted into plasma; a sheath forms around it. Initially electrons dominate collection, charging the probe negatively until no net current, defining floating potential, distinct from plasma potential. The lecture sketches an I-V curve with electron saturation, ion saturation, and regimes A-C, then outlines sheath theory, Debye length, quasi-planar and cold-ion assumptions, continuity and energy conservation, and derives ion and electron currents. Single probes are interpreted by sweeping near floating potential to measure electron temperature from the slope and density from ion saturation current, with limitations including high currents/heating and sweep time. Double probes use two probes biased relative to each other, limiting current to ion saturation; triple probes add a floating probe to measure three curve points without sweeping. Magnetic fields and collisions are noted as added complications.

PATCH is a network growth model extending the Barabási-Albert preferential attachment model by combining triadic closure and homophily. It studies network segregation, degree inequality, and inequity between minority and majority groups. Homophily drives segregation and inequity; preferential attachment drives degree inequality; triadic closure has context-dependent effects, often moderating segregation and inequity but exacerbating degree inequality in most cases. In simulations, the group with more links also shows higher inequality. Applying likelihood-free inference to APS, APS-CIT, and DBLP collaboration and citation networks, the variant in which both global and triadic closure links are biased by preferential attachment and moderate gender homophily best reproduces observed gender inequalities. The passage concludes that reducing network inequalities requires simultaneously addressing homophily, preferential attachment, and triadic closure, while considering possible trade-offs.

Newly analyzed microstructures help explain dandelion seed release. A U.S.-Australian team found a structural quirk that lets batches of seeds catch upward puffs. Imaging showed an off-center, skinny strand tethering each seed, surrounded by horseshoe-shaped shielding. The U-curl steadies the seed unless force tilts it toward the open side; then the tuft’s weight overwhelms the tether, causing lift-off. Measurements found upslanting seeds needed an order of magnitude less force than downward pulling, while pulling straight out was most difficult.

MAFLD, formerly NAFLD, has a global prevalence of 32.4% and is the commonest liver disease. T2D is a major risk factor for MAFLD and is associated with poor liver-related outcomes. Guidelines recommend screening people with diabetes for MAFLD and advanced liver fibrosis, but evidence in Africa is limited; the estimated prevalence of MAFLD among people with T2D in Africa is 30.4%, based on four studies. This study aimed to determine MAFLD prevalence and its association with HbA1c in people with T2D in Africa. The review followed PRISMA, was registered on PROSPERO, searched multiple databases to December 6, 2023, included observational studies of adults with T2D in African countries published in English, and used random-effects meta-analysis. From 659 references, 10 articles were included: nine cross-sectional and one case-control, published 2011–2023, from six African countries. The studies involved 1,667 T2D participants; MAFLD diagnosis was mostly by ultrasonography.

The study used 7 tesla MRS to quantify brain metabolite levels in controls, first-degree biological relatives of individuals with psychosis, and people with a history of psychotic psychopathology (PwPP) in mid-occipital and dorsomedial prefrontal volumes. Among six a priori metabolites, occipital NAA was lower in PwPP and relatives than controls, and prefrontal NAAG differed across groups, tending to be lower in PwPP; other a priori comparisons, including GABA and glutamate, were not significant. Post hoc analyses showed higher prefrontal glucose in PwPP than controls, with a similar nonsignificant trend in occipital cortex. Follow-up analyses indicated occipital NAA remained lower in PwPP versus controls after age, sex, and BMI covariates, while prefrontal NAAG differences did not remain significant. Hierarchical clustering associated glucose with psychiatric and visual-task measures. Repeat scans in a subset showed fair-to-excellent agreement across 16 metabolites. The authors report a pattern of metabolic dysfunction across brain regions in PwPP and, to a lesser extent, in relatives.

The passage discusses the convergence problem of the discrete-time Fourier transform and introduces the Z-transform as a generalization. The Fourier transform converges if a sequence is absolutely summable. The Z-transform uses \(z = r e^{j\omega}\) and converges when \(x[n]r^{-n}\) is absolutely summable. It equals the Fourier transform when \(|z|=1\). For exponential and sum-of-exponential sequences, Z-transforms are ratios of polynomials described by poles and zeros, and they require a region of convergence. Examples show that the same rational expression can have different regions of convergence. Regions of convergence contain no poles and are bounded by poles; finite-length, right-sided, left-sided, and two-sided sequences have specific region types. A stable system’s region includes the unit circle, and a causal system has a right-sided sequence with region outside the outermost pole. The convolution property maps convolution to multiplication. The passage concludes by noting the inverse Z-transform will be covered next.

In Mendez Suarez v. Comfort, the Tenth Circuit reviewed and affirmed the INS’s reinstatement of a prior removal order. Petitioner, a Mexican citizen, was excluded and deported in December 1996 after attempting entry with counterfeit documents at El Paso and illegally reentered in October 1999. After his September 2002 arrest in Colorado on a domestic-violence charge, the INS reinstated the prior order under INA § 241(a)(5), 8 U.S.C. § 1231(a)(5). The district court transferred his habeas petition to the Tenth Circuit under 28 U.S.C. § 1631. The court held transfer was proper and rejected claims that reinstatement deprived him of due process because of bond and state criminal proceedings, that § 1231(a)(5) was retroactively applied, that he was entitled to adjustment of status under the LIFE Act, and that the reinstatement procedure violated due process. It found no prejudice and lacked jurisdiction to review the underlying deportation order.

The study estimated the direct healthcare-related economic burden of PCOS-related mental health disorders through a systematic review and meta-analysis of published human observational studies with control groups, following PRISMA and searching six English databases through July 16, 2021. Twenty-five studies were included. Meta-analysis found higher prevalence ratios for anxiety (1.42; 95% CI 1.32, 1.52), depression (1.65; 95% CI 1.44, 1.89), and eating disorders (1.48; 95% CI 1.06, 2.05) in women with PCOS compared with age-matched women without PCOS. Postpartum depression was not statistically significant (PR 1.20; 95% CI 0.96, 1.50) and was excluded from burden calculations. Estimated excess cases and annual costs in 2021 USD were 216,248 and $1.938 billion for anxiety, 262,176 and $1.678 billion for depression, and 48,764 and $0.644 billion for eating disorders. Trim-and-fill analysis made the eating disorder result non-significant. The combined additional direct healthcare costs associated with depression and anxiety in PCOS were estimated at $4.261 billion/year, with 45% attributable to anxiety, 40% to depression, and the remainder to eating disorders. Total excess economic burden for PCOS was estimated to exceed $15 billion annually, with about 28% from PCOS-related mental health disorders. The passage concludes that improved detection, awareness, and intervention for PCOS and associated disorders would be cost-effective.

This study evaluated expected performance of COVID-19 testing and isolation strategies adopted in France, Belgium, and Italy for winter 2022/2023 using Influenzanet survey responses from 4,594 participants and a mathematical model parameterized to Omicron subvariants. Survey results showed high adherence to testing if symptomatic, lower if asymptomatic, and reduced testing if tests cost up to 20 Euros. Booster willingness differed; the fall booster was estimated to raise vaccine-conferred protection. Modeling with R=1.6 and 75% isolation effectiveness predicted testing and isolation reduced R by 18.4% under the French protocol, 17.2% under the Belgian protocol, and 24.4% under the Italian protocol; none alone reduced R below 1. The Italian protocol was more effective due to longer isolation but had higher social cost in days lost. The Belgian protocol required 0.7 tests per infected person versus 1 and 1.2 for the French and Italian protocols, and simpler isolation guidelines could reduce testing resources without affecting performance. Cost barriers would reduce effectiveness by about 60%. Higher isolation effectiveness improved control but still left R>1; lower effectiveness reduced control. The authors state high fall booster coverage remains imperative, and lower vaccination coverage would compromise testing and isolation impact.

Erik Demaine introduces a class on geometry, folding, algorithms, and the mathematics and algorithms behind folding and unfolding geometric objects. The class covers linkages, paper, and polyhedra; questions are characterized as foldability or design, and results as universality, decision, or hardness. Applications listed include robotics and programmable matter, computer graphics and morphing, mechanics, manufacturing, optics, medical devices and drug delivery, aero-astro deployment, biology and protein folding, sculpture and origami, and reconfigurable buildings and architecture.

For linkages, examples include straight-line mechanisms such as Watt and Peaucellier linkages, a universality result for signing a name with a 2D linkage, an open problem when crossings are forbidden, rigidity questions, and reconfiguration from one configuration to another, which is generally computationally intractable. Universality holds for 2D chains, not for 2D trees or 3D chains and trees; 4D and higher are easy. Locked trees and the knitting-needles example illustrate non-foldability, and characterizing bad 3D chains and 2D trees is open. Protein backbones relate to 3D chains and trees.

For paper, deciding which crease patterns fold flat is NP-hard; single-vertex cases are understood, while folding marked road maps of size 2 by n is open. Design includes universal results that any polygon, polyhedron, or two-color pattern can be folded. Origamizer can produce crease patterns for 3D polyhedra such as the Stanford bunny, though efficiency is unproved. TreeMaker and the tree method design origami bases via a hard disk-packing-related problem, with most efficient use NP-complete. The folding-cut theorem allows any polygon or collection of polygons by one straight cut. Curved creases, self-folding sheets, programmable matter, and universal hinge patterns using box pleating are discussed. Thickness is mostly assumed zero, with Britney Gallivan’s paper-folding analysis as an exception.

For polyhedra, edge unfolding of convex polyhedra is an old open problem going back to Dürer; non-convex polyhedra cannot always be edge-unfolded. General unfolding is always possible for convex polyhedra and orthogonal polyhedra, though the method uses exponentially many cuts; vertex unfolding works for any triangulated surface. Hinged dissections show that any finite set of equal-area polygons can be folded from one chain without collision; this extends to 3D with an extra condition and has applications to sculpture and robot transformers. The class includes lectures, problem sets, a project and presentation, an optional open problem session, and the textbook Geometric Folding Algorithms by Demaine and O’Rourke.

The text introduces a bound-preserving technique coupling cell-centered finite volume (CCFV) and discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods for steady convection-diffusion problems, especially convection-dominated regimes with narrow layers. It reviews stabilization needs and compares CCFV and DG: CCFV is locally conservative, inexpensive, and monotone under two-point flux approximations, but low-order and prone to layer smearing and grid-orientation issues; DG offers high-order accuracy, hp-adaptivity, sharp layer resolution, and parallelization, but more unknowns, parameter tuning, higher cost, and lack of inherent monotonicity. The proposed coupling aims to combine strengths while addressing where to deploy FV versus DG. The new method targets DG overshoots/undershoots: if a DG cell average violates bounds within a tolerance, the approximation reverts to CCFV in a small neighborhood, similar to p-adaptivity. This is intended to yield bound-preserving cell averages up to tolerance without postprocessing; standard conservative slope limiters can then preserve bounds for the full solution. The text also outlines the model PDE, FV/DG domain decomposition, TPFA admissibility, and coupled discretization with jump/average notations.

The lecture demonstrates a C buffer overflow, showing overwritten return addresses and possible code execution. Using effective-Hamiltonian molecular-dynamics simulations, the study investigates topological textures in Zr-substituted BaTiO3 (BZT). In a 12.5% ordered superlattice, chemical doubling along [111] produces alternating textures: one half hosts a −2 antiskyrmion composed of six −1/3 topological quarks, while the other hosts a +4 skyrmion composed of six +2/3 quarks. The two halves share the same vortex geometry, with an integer offset of +1 per vortex. An optional field-theoretic picture describes the doubled cell as a ℤ2 color background imposing a half-translation sign and holonomy. For random Zr substitution from 0% to 12.5%, nanodomains remain inducible and stable at 1 K; disorder pins and distorts vortices, yielding heterogeneous fractionalization and a skyrmion-glass-like state. Thermal ramping shows nontrivial topology persists over broad temperature ranges. Critical temperature is non-monotonic with Zr concentration, initially decreasing with a minimum near 6–8% and partially recovering toward 12.5%; pure BT has highest intrinsic stability, and larger diameters are more robust. Near room temperature, the 12.5% superlattice remains rhombohedral above 300 K. At 293 K, nanodomains cannot be retained without bias, but a local [111] electric field of about 350 kV/cm writes and holds domains with Q=+4 on every (111) projection, with volatile operation and no −2/+4 alternation. The random 12.5% composition under the same bias destabilizes into multidomain states. The work concludes BZT supports ferroelectric topological textures from fractionalized quarks at low temperature to field-stabilized Q=+4 textures near room temperature, and identifies strain, electrostatics, and compositional patterning as promising routes.

The passage discusses functional van der Waals heterostructures for quantum photonics and related applications, focusing on WSe2/CrI3 interfaces. It notes that TMDs and vdW magnets have rich excitonic spectra, and that proximity effects can generate magnetic fields and split nonmagnetic excitonic states. The study uses DFT, QSGW, and QSGŴ methods to examine bilayer and trilayer WSe2/CrI3 structures, including FM and AFM configurations. LDA predicts type II band alignment, while QSGW and QSGŴ predict type I alignment with WSe2-dominated band edges. The WSe2 A and B excitons remain largely confined to WSe2, and CrI3 Frenkel-like magnetic excitons are also observed. In addition, new interlayer excitons appear between the A and B excitons, showing enhanced brightness compared to intralayer CrI3 excitons and robustness across layered and magnetic variants. Magnetic splittings of the A and B excitons depend on band alignments and configuration, with the largest splitting in the FM trilayer. The passage concludes that these heterostructures are promising platforms for in-situ generation and control of interlayer excitonic states, while noting sensitivity to structural and band-alignment details.

The passage argues that the reproduction number measures pathogen spread but does not control for the quantity of tests, making it biased when testing varies over time. It presents the acceleration index from Baunez et al., an elasticity measuring the proportional responsiveness of cases to tests, or the ratio of case growth to test growth. Theoretically, ε = R × A/B, where A is infectivity intensity and B is test intensity. The reproduction number is a special case of the acceleration index and is less accurate when tests vary; R overestimates acceleration when test intensity exceeds infectivity intensity, and underestimates it when test intensity is below infectivity intensity. Using French data from May 13, 2020, to October 26, 2022, and five other countries, the passage reports sizeable differences, with R often underestimating viral spread, especially during Omicron. It concludes that authorities should track the acceleration index alone, or R with test and infectivity intensities, and prefers the acceleration index as a parsimonious, unit-free, test-adjusted indicator. Limitations include dependence on testing and unaccounted cases.

This study examined Ethiopian education policy documents and secondary school principals’ and teachers’ conceptualizations of curriculum differentiation. It analyzed the ETP 2023, GECF 2020, and Guidelines for CD and IEP 2012, and interviewed two school principals and 17 subject teachers from one regular and one special day secondary school. The ETP and GECF conceptualize CD through tracks, fields of study, streams, and school types, while the Guidelines emphasize differentiating curriculum components—content, instructional processes, assessment strategies, and learning environments—in inclusive classrooms. Principals’ and teachers’ conceptualizations varied, showing lack of awareness, divergent views, and alignment with policy intentions. Themes included CD as gifted programs, student placement into subjects/streams/schools, special curriculum for groups, identification and accommodation of gifts and talents, and curricular planning and teaching strategy. The study reports that incoherent policy guidance and limited principal and teacher engagement with reform ideas contributed to these varied conceptualizations. It also states that policy intentions are inadequately addressed by differentiation by school types, such as regular, special day, and boarding schools, which do not match variations in subject types and difficulty levels.

The Cape Horn Pigeon sailed on a whaling voyage on Dec. 7, 1891. On Sept. 10, 1892, while whaling on the high seas of the Okhotsk Sea, it was seized by an Imperial Russian navy officer, taken by force to Vladivostok, and detained until Oct. 1, 1892; the captain protested, the crew was pressed into navigating the Russian vessel, and the arresting officer claimed the Okhotsk Sea was closed. Previously, the bark had called at Vladivostok, where the captain announced his whaling intention and asked permission to enter certain bays after Russia had issued a notice forbidding whaling within 3 miles of the Russian coast or in bays; permission was not granted, but no intimation was given that Russia claimed jurisdiction over the entire Okhotsk Sea. After the captain telegraphed the U.S. legation at St. Petersburg, the Russian ministry informed the U.S. Chargé d’Affaires that the bark had been released.

Using China Education Panel Survey data, this study examines parental education level and child cognitive ability through descriptive statistics and quantitative analysis. The sample included 13,981 students from the 2013–2014 academic year. A multiple linear regression model used parental years of education as core explanatory variables, standardized 3PL cognitive ability test scores as the dependent variable, and various child, family, school, and mediating variables. Findings show a significant positive correlation; one-year increase in the maximum parental education raises child cognitive ability by 0.019 points. Parental education affects cognitive ability via educational expectations and investment. Effects are greater for girls, urban parents, and children with lower cognitive ability, and decline as cognitive ability increases.

The native assembler procedures are stackless and use register passing. One initializes the processor and cache to establish a pre-memory stack before main memory: it divides the stack among cores, maps it to global address space, sets MTRRs on x86-64, runs on all cores, handles protected/real mode SS/ESP, creates UEFI_SEC_PEI_HAND_OFF, and returns AGESA success, warning, or fatal status codes; the host must use it. AARCH64 APUs with PSP do not use the stack/early macros; PSP initializes DRAM. The other removes the pre-memory stack after main memory is available, disables CAR, does not modify MTRR settings, flushes cache lines, runs only on BSP, and returns AGESA_SUCCESS. AmdCreateStruct creates storage for an AGESA call parameter block and pre-initializes it; allocation methods are PreMemHeap, PostMemDram, and ByHost.

The lecture introduces a general relativity course. Its key textbook is Sean Carroll’s general relativity text, with Bernard Schutz’s A First Course in General Relativity as a supplement; Misner, Thorne, and Wheeler’s Gravitation is recommended mainly as a reference, and Wald’s General Relativity is described as terse, formal, and suitable for mathematically minded readers. Grades come entirely from 11 problem sets, with 10 worth 9% and the 11th 10%. The first half of the course covers mathematical foundations and aims to derive the Einstein field equations by the week before spring break; the second half applies them to Newtonian gravity, classic tests, cosmology, black holes, gravitational waves, and neutron stars. The lecture begins special relativity from a geometric viewpoint. It defines spacetime as a manifold of events with a metric, explains manifolds, events, and metrics, and introduces inertial reference frames as freely moving lattices of uniformly ticking clocks and measuring rods, with clocks synchronized by the Einstein procedure using the constancy of light speed. Units are chosen so c = 1. It discusses displacement vectors between events, Lorentz transformations between inertial observers, index notation and the summation convention, and defines spacetime vectors as quartets of components transforming like displacement vectors.

This paper investigates whether low dose mammography, at approximately 10% of standard dose, can be used for mammographic density and therefore risk estimation in younger women using deep learning. It compares low dose and standard dose density predictions on the ALDRAM dataset, which contains paired standard and low dose mammograms from women aged 31–45 with unilateral breast cancer. Models are trained on the PROCAS standard dose dataset and on simulated low dose images generated from PROCAS. ResNet-18 models are trained separately for standard and simulated low dose data, and predictions are compared on ALDRAM using Spearman rank correlation and root mean squared error.

The results show that low dose and standard dose predictions are highly similar, especially when averaging across CC and MLO views and across multiple models. Variation between CC and MLO views at the same dose may be as large as same-view variation across doses. No relationship is found between prediction differences and age or dose ratio. Performance is poorer at higher density and smaller breast area; image size differences appear related to breast area. Larger CC–MLO differences and larger differences between repeated low dose models are associated with larger standard–low dose differences. No notable outliers are found, but systematic differences remain, with low dose predictions generally lower than standard dose predictions. The authors conclude that low dose density prediction is feasible but that correction may be needed for factors such as breast area and density.

The passage examines concerns about ultra-processed food and the need for objective processing metrics. It introduces FPro, a continuous machine-learning Food Processing Score generated by FoodProX from 12 nutrition-facts nutrients and trained using NOVA labels. FPro ranges from 0 for unprocessed foods to 1 for ultra-processed foods and can accommodate other classification systems. The authors present GroceryDB, an open-source database of over 50,000 products from Walmart, Target, and WholeFoods online platforms, collected in May 2021. FPro distributions are similar across stores, but WholeFoods offers more minimally processed and fewer ultra-processed items, while Target has a high fraction of ultra-processed offerings. FPro varies by food category. GroceryDB distributions follow trends similar to USDA FNDDS and BFPD, with only 44% overlap with BFPD and less than 30% with Open Food Facts. Higher FPro is associated with cheaper calories overall, though the relationship varies by category. Store offerings differ in processing choices and ingredients; WholeFoods cereals use less sugar, natural flavors, added vitamins, and corn syrup. Ingredient lists are organized as trees, and products with complex trees are more processed. IgFPro ranks ingredients by contribution to processing, identifying certain oils and additives as high or low signals. The discussion states GroceryDB and FPro can inform consumers and policymakers, support substitutions, reformulation, and public health initiatives. Limitations include reliance on nutrition facts, limited ingredient data, and FPro partly drawing from expertise-based classifications. Code and data are available at the BarabasiLab GitHub repository and TrueFood.Tech.

Tecomaria capensis, family Bignoniaceae, is a Cape Honeysuckle/Kaapse Kanferfoelie/Trompetters/Icakatha/Umsilingi, a popular garden and hedging plant that is deciduous in cold areas. It is a scrambling shrub or small tree up to 6 m with opposite compound leaves and orange-red to pale orange trumpet-shaped flowers throughout the year. It is listed as Least Concern and occurs in thicket and forest margins in southern, eastern and tropical Africa. It is browsed by game and stock; visited by sunbirds, butterflies and honey-bees; and its leaves are eaten by death’s head and fulvous hawkmoth larvae. It is used in traditional medicine and its wood is used for isixhoxho. Growing advice includes well-drained soil, compost and fertiliser, mulch, regular water until established, late-winter pruning, and pinching back for a self-standing shrub.

The Special Group (Augmented) oversaw Operation Mongoose, aimed at overthrowing Castro; Lansdale coordinated CIA, State, and Defense, while CIA units in Washington and Miami implemented military, sabotage, and propaganda operations. A Special Group (CI) was created in 1962 for counter-insurgency, and in 1966 Johnson assigned overseas counterinsurgency coordination to the Secretary of State. In 1964, Special Group 5412 became the 303 Committee without changing composition, functions, or responsibility. The Special Group and the 303 Committee approved 163 covert actions under Kennedy and 142 under Johnson through February 1967, but the Church Committee estimated only 14 percent of CIA projects since 1961 were reviewed case-by-case. Nixon required annual reviews in 1969; NSDM 40 in 1970 renamed the group the 40 Committee, added the Attorney General, and reaffirmed DCI responsibility. The 40 Committee considered about 25 percent of projects, and Nixon instructed the DCI to promote a coup in Chile without Committee approval. The 1974 Hughes-Ryan amendment required explicit presidential approval for each action and expanded congressional oversight.

This lecture discusses the economics of spam and security. It contrasts ideologically motivated attacks, which lack a strong economic disincentive, with economically motivated computer crime. Spam is presented as an attack that stops if unprofitable. Examples include Chinese text-message cars, whose antenna costs about $1,600, can generate about $1,600 profit per day, and face fines under $5,000, while Chinese carriers profit from 106-prefix numbers; cyber arms dealers sell exploits, and marketplaces exist for compromised systems, tools, and stolen user information. The spam ecosystem is divided into advertising, click support, and realization. Advertising is very cheap despite low click and purchase rates. Defenses include IP blacklists, email micropayments, computational puzzles, and CAPTCHAs, but attackers evade them using botnets, compromised webmail accounts, BGP hijacks, DNS redirection, fast flux, bulletproof hosting, P2P command-and-control, and cheap human CAPTCHA solving. Click support requires domains, DNS servers, and web servers, often using redirection and decentralized affiliate providers. Realization uses a payment workflow among customers, merchants, payment processors, acquiring banks, association networks, and issuing banks. Spammers classify transactions properly, send goods, and avoid chargebacks because of fines, limited acquiring banks, and Visa policy changes. The passage also addresses ethical concerns in spam research and companies conducting hackbacks.

In a memorandum, the district court denied Defendant Willie Tyler’s motions to dismiss the indictment and bar retrial after his convictions on Counts II and III were vacated and a new trial was ordered based on the investigation-related communications provision. The court rejected the Sixth Amendment Confrontation Clause claim, concluding that David Fones’s hearsay statement about Doreen Proctor was admissible for a purpose other than proving the truth of the matter asserted. It rejected the Fifth Amendment Double Jeopardy claim because the dual sovereignty principle permits state and federal prosecutions and because the convictions were vacated for legal error, not insufficient evidence. It also rejected the Due Process claim based on outrageous government conduct, finding no support that the government invented Diller’s status as a DEA adviser or consultant, and finding that Defendant failed to establish a Brady claim or intentional misconduct warranting dismissal. The motions were denied.

After Hurricane Helene in September 2024, four western North Carolina school buildings flooded severely. In HCPS, Atkinson Elementary flooded, operated from the Boys & Girls Club until December 2024, then returned after new flooring and drainage/vegetation improvements; community partnerships continued. In McDowell County, Old Fort Elementary closed until the 2025-26 school year, merged with PGES, received renovations, and reopened Aug. 25. In Watauga County, Valle Crucis School flooded about 70%; students were housed at ASU, Holy Cross Episcopal Church, and CCCTI while a new school was delayed by construction workforce shortages. Preschool students moved back, and FEMA/insurance funding is being sought for the dry historic rock facade. After moving from Berlin to California, Sara Zaske’s daughter Sophia became the only fourth grader in her class without a smartphone; in Berlin, almost no third graders owned cell phones. Zaske plans to give Sophia a flip phone next year but wait until high school for a smartphone. A 2015 study of about 3,500 European children found 46% of ages 9 to 16 owned a smartphone, with country differences in school restrictions and cost sensitivity. A Nielsen report found about 45% of US children 10 to 12 had their own smartphone with a service plan, and Common Sense Media found 42% of US children 8 and younger had tablets. Outside the US and Europe, first phones tend to come later: in South Korea, about 72% of children owned a smartphone by ages 11 to 12; in Taiwan, use rose from 45% of 11-year-olds to about 71% of 15-year-olds. Turkish parents disagreed on the optimal age. In South Africa, 81% of secondary students had mobile phone access; in Ghana and Malawi, ownership was lower but rose from 2007 to 2014. In Australia, 31% of fourth-year primary children owned or used a phone at the study’s start, 43% did a year later, and the median first age was 8. The American Academy of Pediatrics says there is no “right” age, recommending limits for young children and screen-free times.

This lecture introduces a quantum field theory (QFT) course whose goal is to develop concepts, formalism, and techniques for quantum dynamics of fields, culminating in quantum electrodynamics. QFT describes three of the four fundamental interactions, can be used for some quantum gravity questions but not a complete description, and has applications in condensed matter and statistical physics. The course is the first of a three-semester sequence; QFT 1 covers fundamental concepts, while QFT 2 and 3 are more technical. The outline is rough and may change. The professor calls QFT conceptually difficult but not inherently so if learned correctly, advising that it is quantum mechanics with infinitely many degrees of freedom, that formalisms address concrete physical problems, and that intuition is built through examples; notations may differ from recommended textbooks.

The lecture begins classical field theory with the principle of locality: effects propagate from point to neighboring point, not by action at a distance. Fields assign dynamical variables to each spatial point, with x as a label and t describing evolution. Maxwell’s equations and Einstein gravity are local examples. Field types include scalar, vector, tensor, and spinor. The action for fields is the time integral of a Lagrangian, whose density depends on fields and their derivatives at a single point. Locality forbids terms involving different points, and only first time derivatives are allowed. Extremizing the action gives the field equation of motion. Restricting to translationally and Lorentz-invariant theories, examples include Maxwell theory, Einstein gravity, and scalar field theory. For a real scalar field, the action has kinetic and potential terms; its momentum and Hamiltonian densities are defined. A linear potential gives an external force, while a quadratic potential gives the Klein-Gordon equation.

The passage studies quantum algorithms for generalized linear model (GLM) sparsification. It defines GLM sparsification and proper loss functions, presents a quantum framework for constructing ε-approximate sparsifiers via multiscale leverage score overestimates and quantum importance sampling, and applies this to linear, multiple, ridge, Lasso, Huber, ℓp, and γp regression. The framework achieves quadratic speedups in the number of data points m over classical algorithms and subsumes some prior quantum results for linear, multiple, and ridge regression.

Digital Foundry found Monster Hunter World technically mixed across PS4 and Xbox consoles. Base PS4 uses 1080p with uncapped frame rates often below and occasionally above 30 fps; the other basic-console version is 864p with lower performance. On PS4 Pro and Xbox One X, Resolution mode uses 1800p checkerboard on Pro and 1728p on One X, with missing distant assets on One X and better performance on Pro. Frame-rate mode is 1080p on both, with missing One X assets but generally higher, inconsistent One X frame rates. Graphics mode is 1080p on both, One X assets appear, and One X performs better. The conclusion is that MHW is a technical disappointment, poorly optimized for Pro and especially One X, despite enjoyable gameplay.

The Flex offense is a screening game using strong baseline and down screens. Required fundamentals include passing, base screens, down screens, and back cuts. The passage outlines schematic sequences including basic continuity, ball reversal, corner pass/post isolation, bump back, back cut against overplay, weakside lob, and back-door play. Entries include high post rub, shuffle cut, and dribble clear, plus a “Pop” weakside double screen variation. Offensive rebounding must be stressed because shooters often receive the ball going away from the basket; it requires anticipation, determination, hustle, aggressiveness, second and third efforts, and anticipating missed shots.

This study used SEER Research Plus 2000–2018 data to examine mortality and predict overall survival among patients with soft-tissue sarcomas, including heart cancer, in the United States. The analysis included 24,849 STS patients. Patients averaged 59 years at diagnosis; 56% were male and 82% were white. Liposarcoma was the most prevalent selected sarcoma, while spindle cell sarcoma was least common. Myxofibrosarcoma patients had higher overall survival than other sarcoma patients, while spindle cell sarcoma patients had lower survival. In multivariate analysis, increasing age, male sex, non-white race, advanced cancer stage, and higher tumor grade negatively affected survival. Surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy significantly reduced mortality, while primary systemic therapy had contradictory results. Metastatic disease was associated with a 3.66-fold higher hazard of death than primary stages. The study developed all-cause mortality nomograms to estimate 5- and 10-year overall survival probabilities for patients receiving specific treatments; calibration matched predicted and observed probabilities. Limitations included unavailable clinicopathological factors, no recurrence data, lack of radiotherapy technique details, potential confounding, short follow-up, and need for external validation. The authors conclude that surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy were associated with better survival, while primary systemic therapy had conflicting results, and that a nomogram was developed to predict overall survival.

In MIT 14.271, Glenn Ellison introduces industrial organization, noting the course is co-taught with Tobias and includes Jean Tirole lectures. He says most lectures will be his, and the course covers IO theory and empirical work, with theory on Wednesdays and empirical work on Mondays. He argues IO is inherently theoretical and discusses monopoly pricing: a monopolist sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost and uses the Lerner index, with markup equal to the negative inverse of demand elasticity. He covers deadweight loss and other concerns such as productive inefficiency, quality distortions, rent seeking, and equity, and notes IO generally uses quasilinear preferences.

For multiproduct monopoly, pricing considers diversion ratios and should be treated as a system; substitutes raise markups above the single-product Lerner index, while complements can lead to below-cost pricing to increase sales of profitable goods, with printers/ink, newspapers, and Google as examples. On product quality, a monopolist equates the cost of quality to the marginal consumer’s benefit, while a social planner uses the average consumer, though in homogeneous populations monopolist quality is socially optimal.

For durable goods, a monopolist with commitment power may sell at the monopoly price early and not lower price later. Without commitment, forward-looking consumers can cause prices to fall over time and profits to be lower; the Coase conjecture says profits can go to zero as price adjustment becomes frequent, but the passage lists reasons this may not occur. Information design is introduced through examples of firms controlling product information; suppressing information can homogenize consumers, increase monopoly profit, and sometimes affect consumer surplus. The next class will discuss empirical papers by Chevalier-Goolsbee and Gentzkow-Shapiro.

The lecture presents natural examples of sandwich structures and efficient mechanical design. Monocotyledon leaves such as iris, cattail/bullrush, and grasses have stiff sclerenchyma fibers on the outside and parenchyma or web-like cores inside; iris leaves were tested as sandwich beams using deflection equations, measured geometry, and estimates of face and core moduli, giving calculated stiffness in the same order of magnitude as measured values. Other examples include sea kelp with honeycomb-like cores and gas-filled pockets for buoyancy; bird skulls with foam or trabecular bone between faces; cuttlefish bone/shell with gas pockets used to control buoyancy; and horseshoe crab and Galapagos tortoise shells. The lecture also notes owl skull bone asymmetry and ear height differences, and fox head tilting, as related to locating prey. It then discusses palm stems, which do not increase diameter as they grow taller but add cell-wall layers, producing a radial density gradient with denser material at the periphery. Using Paul Rich’s measurements and analysis, the lecture reports that density varies with radius squared, modulus with density to the 2.5 power, and strength with density squared; that the gradient makes the stem about 2.5 times stiffer than a uniform-density stem of the same mass; and that strength distribution approximately matches bending stress. Bamboo is mentioned as another example.

This paper studies Temperature Scaling (TS) as a post-hoc calibration method for deep-learning brain tumor classification from MRI. It reviews calibration in medical imaging and variants such as Local TS, Attended TS, adaptive/entropy-based methods. The proposed lightweight CNN uses four convolutional layers, ReLU, max-pooling, two fully connected layers, and dropout, and is trained on a composite dataset from Figshare, SARTAJ, and Br35H at 256×256×3. TS divides logits by a scalar temperature optimized by minimizing NLL on validation data. Five synthetic noises are tested: Gaussian, Poisson, Salt & Pepper, Speckle, and Uniform. Metrics include accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, NLL, and ECE. In the baseline no-noise setting, TS did not improve accuracy, F1, recall, or precision and slightly reduced them. Under noise, TS consistently reduced NLL and ECE while preserving classification metrics. Optimal temperatures varied by noise type and level. Tests with ResNet50 under selected noise parameters also showed TS reduced NLL/ECE and improved false positive and false negative rates without affecting overall accuracy. The paper concludes TS is simple, efficient, and improves model reliability under noise while maintaining prediction quality, and future work will test larger datasets, more models, and other calibration methods.

The lecture finishes Cantor’s theorem that any set A has cardinality strictly smaller than its power set, proving an injection from A to P(A) and deriving a contradiction from assuming a bijection via the set B = {x in A : x not in g(x)}. It concludes there are infinitely many infinite sizes. The lecture then introduces the goal of describing R as the unique ordered field containing Q with the least upper bound property. It defines ordered sets, examples and non-examples, upper and lower bounds, supremum and infimum, and the least upper bound property. It states that Z has this property but Q does not, because the set of positive rationals whose square is less than 2 would have no supremum in Q. It begins proving that if x is a rational supremum of this set, then x ≥ 1 and x squared equals 2; it rules out x squared less than 2 and stops before ruling out x squared greater than 2.

This case study examined two middle grades teacher candidates in a year-long Professional Development School experience, focusing on how they viewed, experienced, and used translanguaging with multilingual young adolescent learners and how their middle grades ESL coursework prepared them for translanguaging. The passage reviews literature describing translanguaging as an integrated, asset-based use of multilingual learners’ full linguistic repertoires, distinct from code switching, and discusses monolingual norms, middle grades education, belonging, and the need for teachers to intentionally support multilingual learners. Data included course-related field notes, four rounds of semi-structured interviews, classroom observations and supervision notes, analyzed through a case study approach with coding and contrastive analysis. Findings centered on two themes: teacher candidates’ preparedness and challenges in using translanguaging. Both participants reported positive, asset-based views of translanguaging and felt their coursework provided strategies and tools, but they struggled to apply them in practice. Challenges included discomfort working with multilingual learners, limited experience, and not seeing cooperating teachers model translanguaging; one participant sought outside resources while the other felt unprepared and hesitated to use languages other than English. The study reports a theory-practice gap despite clinical hours, ESL endorsement work, and coursework. The discussion states that having tools and positive mindsets did not necessarily lead to implementing translanguaging and recommends professional development and training for cooperating teachers so candidates can see translanguaging practiced. The conclusion calls for teacher preparation programs and middle grades educators to create linguistically inclusive spaces, provide professional development on translanguaging, and conduct more research and training focused on translanguaging in the middle grades.

Divergence in trading occurs when price swings and indicator movement are not in phase: price makes a higher swing high while an oscillator makes a lower high, or price makes a lower swing low while the indicator makes a higher swing low. A divergence trading strategy uses price action and oscillators such as RSI, MACD, Stochastic Oscillator, or CCI to identify potential reversals or momentum shifts. Bullish divergence is price lower lows and oscillator higher lows; bearish divergence is price higher highs and oscillator lower highs. Divergence is broadly classified as classical/regular and hidden. Classical divergence forms against the prevailing trend and may indicate reversal, temporary pullback, or continuation after a multiple-legged pullback. Hidden divergence forms during pullbacks and may indicate trend continuation, though it can occur at trend end with head-and-shoulders or inverse head-and-shoulders patterns. The passage backtests a simple divergence strategy on SPY/S&P 500, using optimization of days/settings, profit factor, Sharpe Ratio, and equity curve; results show favorable profit factor from about 2 to 20 days, low max drawdowns, 2012 as only losing year, and relatively few trades. Examples include classical bullish Nasdaq 100 March 2020, hidden bullish TSLA March 2020, classical bearish S&P 500 February 2020, and hidden bearish Nasdaq 100 December 2018, each with candlestick triggers. The passage also discusses advantages, volume analysis as confirmation, common mistakes such as misunderstanding divergence, relying solely on signals, overtrading, poor risk management, and emotional decisions, and stresses backtesting and risk management.

Layout guidance advises using short, direct, thick high-current power traces, at least 15 mils per ampere; placing the inductor, output capacitors, and output diode close together; connecting IC, input/output capacitor, and diode grounds close to a ground plane; and using ground planes on both PCB sides or separate planes on multilayer boards.
